analysis.one_liner: Caps spill liability for Great Lakes oil pipelines at $75 million, requires spill insurance, and lets regulators order shutdowns.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a vote or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill changes how oil pipelines that cross the Great Lakes are held financially accountable for spills. It caps a pipeline owner's spill liability at cleanup costs plus $75 million, the same cap that already applies to offshore pipelines, and requires owners to prove they have insurance or a bond to cover that amount. It also expands the Transportation Department's power to order a hazardous-liquid pipeline to shut down or fix problems without a hearing, including when the pipeline is violating conditions it agreed to with a state, tribal, or local government, or when cleanup resources would be inadequate in winter or extreme weather. At the same time, it takes away the Department's existing emergency-order power over natural gas pipelines.
analysis.who_benefits: People who depend on the Great Lakes for drinking water, fishing, and tourism benefit from the bill's shutdown authority, which targets pipelines carrying oil through the lakes, and from the requirement that operators prove they hold insurance or a bond to pay for a spill. State, tribal, and local governments also gain a new enforcement hook: regulators could order a pipeline to comply with conditions the operator previously agreed to with those governments.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Great Lakes communities and water users

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires the responsible party for a Great Lakes pipeline to establish and maintain evidence of financial responsibility, such as insurance or a bond, so that money is guaranteed to be available if a spill happens.

It lets the Transportation Department issue an emergency order, without prior notice or a hearing, when it finds reliable evidence that a hazardous-liquid pipeline is violating operating conditions the responsible party previously agreed to with a state, tribal, or local government.

It lets the Transportation Department, after consulting the EPA and Coast Guard, order fixes or insurance when cleanup resources are inadequate during seasonal conditions or extreme weather, or when the operator cannot show it has the financial resources to meet the liability limits.

analysis.who_pays: Oil pipeline operators with Great Lakes crossings would bear the cost of maintaining insurance or bonds and would face the risk of emergency shutdown orders. Because the bill caps their liability at cleanup costs plus $75 million, if a catastrophic spill cost more than that, the excess would fall on the federal Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund and ultimately taxpayers rather than the operator. Natural gas pipelines gain relief, since they would no longer face the Department's emergency-order authority.
analysis.who_pays_short: Great Lakes oil pipeline operators; taxpayers above the cap

drawbacks.text: The bill caps a Great Lakes pipeline operator's spill liability at all cleanup costs plus $75 million, equalizing it with offshore pipelines, even though current law imposes unlimited liability on onshore facilities; a spill costing far more than the cap, which is plausible for a major Great Lakes pipeline rupture, would leave the excess to be covered by the public Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund instead of the company.

The bill eliminates the Transportation Department's existing emergency-order authority over natural gas pipelines, removing a tool the Department can currently use to address imminent hazards from gas pipelines without prior notice or a hearing.
The new shutdown authority applies only to hazardous-liquid pipelines and only in limited situations, so it would not cover other safety problems an inspector might identify outside those conditions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The shutdown authority and the insurance requirement address a real and severe risk: an oil spill into the Great Lakes, the source of drinking water for a large region, would be extremely costly and hard to clean up, especially in winter ice conditions. But the bill's headline liability figure cuts the operator's maximum exposure well below what a catastrophic spill could cost, shifting the worst-case bill to the public. The gas-pipeline carve-out weakens oversight elsewhere. An honest supporter would have to acknowledge that the liability cap is a significant concession bundled with the safety provisions.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced and never came back out, so no vote was ever held before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Gary Peters introduced the LINES Act in the Senate on May 24, 2017, with Sen. Debbie Stabenow as cosponsor.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works on the day of introduction.
No further action was ever taken: the committee never reported the bill, and no vote occurred in either chamber before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Great Lakes oil pipeline operators are better off, because the status quo held: they face no new insurance mandate, no emergency shutdown authority, and also no cap limiting their currently unlimited spill liability. Natural gas pipeline operators also keep the emergency-order oversight the bill would have removed.

sides.party_line_note: Only two Democrats, both from Michigan, sponsored the bill, and the Republican-led committee never acted on it, but no votes or stated opposition appear in the record, so the partisan split cannot be measured.

industries.industry: Oil pipeline operators crossing the Great Lakes
industries.note: The bill would both constrain and shield these operators: it adds mandatory insurance, new shutdown authority, and compliance orders, but it caps spill liability at cleanup costs plus $75 million where current law leaves onshore-facility liability unlimited. A catastrophic spill could cost far more than the cap, with the public fund absorbing the excess.

The bill eliminates the Transportation Department's emergency-order authority over gas pipelines, a tool currently available to address imminent hazards without prior notice. That removes a safety lever the public retains today.

The financial-responsibility mandate would require Great Lakes pipeline operators to obtain insurance or bonds, creating new demand for spill-liability coverage and giving the public a guaranteed source of cleanup funds.
